explanations.explanation: A fig tree, friend, just like Mark says. Jesus spots it in the distance, covered in leaves, and walks over to look for fruit. I think a tree in leaf looks promising from far off. It's like a cookie box that looks full from across the room and turns out to hold nothing but crumbs.

Olive tree is a decent guess, friend, but Mark names a different tree. The tree Jesus walks toward is a fig tree in leaf. He goes to see if there's any fruit on it. Keep that fig tree in your pocket, because it comes back later.

Ooh, you're reaching for a famous tree there. Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, climbed up a sycamore-fig tree to see Jesus (Luke 19:2-4). But the tree in this story is a fig tree. Jesus sees it in leaf from a distance and goes to look for fruit.

I get why you'd hope so, friend. But when Jesus reaches the tree, Mark says He found nothing on it except leaves. No figs at all, hiding or otherwise. The reason is right there in the text: it was not the season for figs.
False is right, friend. Jesus reaches the tree and finds nothing on it except leaves. No sneaky figs tucked behind a branch. Mark tells us it was not the season for figs.

explanations.answer: May no one ever eat its fruit again
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says to the tree, “May no one ever eat of your fruit again.” Notice He's talking right to the tree. That's a strange thing to see, and I think the disciples were watching closely.

explanations.answer: May it be full of figs by morning
explanations.explanation: I like the hopeful spirit, friend, but that's not what Jesus says. He tells the tree, “May no one ever eat of your fruit again.” And when morning comes, the tree is withered from its roots, not loaded with figs (Mark 11:20).

explanations.answer: May it be cut down before evening
explanations.explanation: Close on the mood, friend, but not on the words. Jesus never mentions cutting the tree down. He says, “May no one ever eat of your fruit again.” The next morning the disciples see the tree withered from its roots (Mark 11:20).
True, friend. Mark says it plainly: “And His disciples heard this statement.” So they heard what Jesus said to the tree. That matters when we get to the next morning.
Not quite, friend. Mark says, “And His disciples heard this statement.” So they heard what Jesus said to the tree. Mark tells us they heard it, and that's the part to hold on to.

explanations.answer: He begins to drive them out
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jesus enters the temple courts and begins to drive out those who were buying and selling there. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. I think that got everybody's attention.

explanations.answer: He sits down and watches them
explanations.explanation: No sitting and watching here, friend. Mark says Jesus began to drive out those who were buying and selling in the temple courts. He overturned tables and seats, too. That's a whole lot of action for someone who's supposed to be just looking around.

explanations.answer: He buys a dove for an offering
explanations.explanation: Doves are in the story, friend, but Jesus isn't shopping. He begins to drive out those who were buying and selling there. He even overturns the seats of those selling doves. That's about as far from a shopping trip as you can get.
That's the one, baker. Mark says Jesus “…overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves.” Money changers it is. I think that courtyard got loud in a hurry.

Tax collectors are a good guess, friend, but they aren't in this scene. Mark says Jesus “…overturned the tables of the money changers…” Those are the tables that go over, and the seats of the dove sellers go too.

Temple guards sound official, friend, and I'd have guessed them too. But Mark doesn't mention any guards here. The tables Jesus overturns belong to the money changers, and the seats of those selling doves go over as well. No guards in the verse, so I'm not adding any, not even for drama.
Merchandise it is, friend. Mark says Jesus would not allow anyone to carry merchandise through the temple courts. Notice that it's anyone, not just the sellers. He wouldn't allow it.
Good thinking, friend, since offerings fit a temple. But Mark's word is different. Jesus would not allow anyone to carry merchandise through the temple courts. Merchandise is what He stops.

No weapons in this verse, friend. Mark says He would not allow anyone to carry merchandise through the temple courts. Merchandise is the word, so goods, not swords. Weapons would make this a very different story, and Mark doesn't tell that one.

explanations.answer: A house of prayer for all the nations
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Jesus asks, “Is it not written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’?” That's what He points them back to. Prayer, and room for all the nations.

explanations.answer: A house of offering for the priests
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, friend, but it's not what Jesus quotes. He says, “My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations…” Prayer is the name, and it's for all the nations. The priests aren't in that line.

explanations.answer: A house of gold for the kings
explanations.explanation: Fancy guess, friend, but gold and kings aren't in the verse. Jesus asks what is written: “My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations…” That's the name He points to. Simple as that, and big enough for everyone.

That's what He says, baker. After the house of prayer line, Jesus tells them, “But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’…” It's a sharp contrast with what the house was meant to be. Prayer on one side, a den of robbers on the other.
Lions are in another famous story, friend. Daniel was thrown into a den of lions (Daniel 6:16). But that's not what Jesus says here. He says they've made God's house “a den of robbers.”
Idols don't come up in this scene, friend. Jesus says, “But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’…” That's the phrase He uses. Stay with His words and you can't go off the path.
Yes, friend, and it's a heavy one. Mark says the chief priests and scribes looked for a way to kill Him. I think this is a part where we slow down and let it sit. The story is getting serious.
I wish the verse went that way, friend. It doesn't. After they heard Jesus, the chief priests and scribes looked for a way to kill Him. It's a heavy moment in the story.
Following Him isn't what they're up to, friend. Mark says they looked for a way to kill Him. That's a heavy line. I think it's the moment the story turns dark.

Not quite, friend. Mark gives a different reason: they were afraid of Him because the whole crowd was astonished at His teaching. Mark says astonished, not turned against Him. The crowd's amazement is the reason Mark gives for their fear.
False is right, friend. Mark says they were afraid of Him, because the whole crowd was astonished at His teaching. So the crowd is amazed, not turning away. The fear comes from that.

Withered, friend, and all the way down. Mark says they saw the fig tree withered from its roots. Peter remembers it and calls it the tree Jesus cursed. That's quite a change from the leaves Jesus saw on it earlier.

Budding would be a happy surprise, friend, but that's not the scene. Mark says they saw the fig tree withered from its roots. It's the same tree Jesus spoke to the day before. It looks very different now.

Blooming would be a plot twist, friend, but this story goes the other way. The disciples see the fig tree withered from its roots. Peter remembers and says it's the tree Jesus cursed. Withered from the roots is not a tree having an off day.

Peter, friend, one of Jesus' disciples. Mark says Peter remembered it and said, “Look, Rabbi! The fig tree You cursed has withered.” He's the one who connects the tree to what Jesus said the day before. Good memory on that man.

Thomas is one of the twelve, friend (Mark 3:18), but he's not the one speaking here. Mark says Peter remembered it and spoke up. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, points out the tree. Thomas will have to wait for another passage.

Andrew is one of the twelve, friend (Mark 3:18), but he's not the one talking this time. Mark says Peter remembered it and said, “Look, Rabbi!” Peter is another of Jesus' disciples. He's the one who speaks up about the tree.
That's it, baker. Jesus tells them, “Have faith in God…” Peter points at a tree, and Jesus points them to God. Everything else in this part grows out of that line.
Fear isn't the word Jesus uses here, friend. Right after Peter points out the tree, Jesus says, “Have faith in God…” That's the whole line. It's an invitation to trust.
Waiting quietly sounds peaceful, friend, but it's not what Jesus says. He answers Peter with “Have faith in God…” Then He keeps going with more to say. Faith is what He puts first.

That's not how Jesus says it, friend. He says the mountain gets thrown into the sea if the one speaking “…has no doubt in his heart but believes that it will happen…” Doubt isn't part of that picture. Believing is.
False is right, friend. Jesus says it will be done for the one who “…has no doubt in his heart but believes that it will happen…” So doubt isn't in the picture. Belief is what He describes.

explanations.answer: Believe that you have received it
explanations.explanation: That's what He says, baker. Jesus tells them, “…whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.” He moves the mountain picture straight into prayer. Believe, and it will be yours.

explanations.answer: Keep asking until a sign comes
explanations.explanation: I understand wanting a sign, friend, but Jesus doesn't say that here. He says, “…whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.” The instruction is to believe. No sign is mentioned.

Mornings are in this story, friend, but not in this instruction. Jesus says, “…whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.” Nothing about waiting for the next day. He tells them to believe.

explanations.answer: Forgive what you hold against them
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, “…if you hold anything against another, forgive it, so that your Father in heaven will forgive your trespasses as well.” He says it for the moment you stand to pray. It's a simple instruction, and it's not an easy one.

Priests aren't in this instruction, friend. Jesus says, “…if you hold anything against another, forgive it, so that your Father in heaven will forgive your trespasses as well.” Forgiving is the step He gives. He ties it to your Father forgiving your trespasses.

Waiting for an apology is a very human move, friend. I'd probably be standing there with my mustache crossed. But Jesus doesn't say to wait. He says, “…if you hold anything against another, forgive it…”

True, friend. Jesus says to forgive, “…so that your Father in heaven will forgive your trespasses as well.” He ties the two together in the same sentence. It's a lot to take in, and it's worth reading slowly.

He does connect them, friend. Jesus says to forgive anything you hold against another “…so that your Father in heaven will forgive your trespasses as well.” Both are in the same sentence. Forgiving others and the Father forgiving your trespasses go together there.
